utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Scott, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Scott: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good sir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions about the 9th of May, 1993, please. And you may recall yesterday we spoke about Vinko Martinovic, Stela, and how you saw him once early in the morning or running by and then later that afternoon or evening around 4.00 or 5.00. I want to ask you now, sir: Do you recall whether you saw any other members of the Martinovic family on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that morning, I didn't see anyone else. I saw the five or six of them whom I knew. I don't know who else I could have seen. I know his brother, but I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The woman who you said came to you complaining about being evicted by Stela and then you told us the story about how it wasn't Stela and in fact, Stela was there with you at the time -- you said that this happened, if I heard you correctly, sir, in the winter of 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is misinterpreted. No one was expelled from a flat. We -- it had to do with 100 marks. That was about October. I know that work was being carried out inside, not in the yard. No one was expelled from a flat. This had to do with the 100 marks that were taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Maybe we're talking about the same event, sir, and maybe we're not. So let me see if I understand. You recall the incidents where you told us that a woman came to you making allegation that is something had happened to her that had been done by Stela; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us, in fact, that when she described this person who she claimed to be Stela, that it -- the physical description she gave was not in fact Stela. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, it happened to be that, according to you, Stela was with you at that time, at the moment of this conversation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He wasn't with me, but he was with some others. He was in company probably from the town defence. He was sitting with them and I was serving. I wasn't sitting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So what happened on that occasion was not that the woman had claimed to be -- that she was being evicted or had been evicted someone but that some money had been taken from her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. She claimed that she had been threatened with a gun and told to give her money or she would be killed and that he introduced himself as Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, thank you for that clarification and my misunderstanding. You said that it was clear that it was not Stela that was involved in this, but do you know, for instance, sir -- do you know that it wasn't Stela's soldiers who had done that thing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given the description she gave, she said he had black hair and had a ponytail. It couldn't have been any one of his men because at the time they all had short hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your conclusion -- again, just so it's clear, sir, your conclusion is that none of these soldiers were Stela's men is based entirely on the physical description given by this woman; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's based on the description that she gave and also on the location of the event, because it took place near the Mostarka building, which is about 2 kilometres from my building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, didn't soldiers have the ability to move in fact all over West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, when they had the time. But as there weren't enough of them, they probably didn't have -- well, some of them remained in the base. Some of them were at positions. I can't exclude that possibility. He could have been wearing a wig. But according to the description, he had black hair and was wear ago ponytail, so this description didn't correspond to anyone from that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, going to these prisoners who stayed at the headquarters and were fed, not at your restaurant, as you described it, but by -- excuse me, with food from your restaurant. If I understood you correctly, sir, you said that there were approximately from 5 to 12 prisoners who you would feed in the way you described. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there were about -- between 5 and 12, maybe sometimes 15 soldiers. I can't remember exactly. I didn't count them. And I wasn't there all the time either. They were given the same food that the soldiers were given, and I said that they were about 3 metres away, because there was only a corridor with flowers which separated them -- a part with flowers that separated them, and that still exists today. So about 3 or 4 metres away they had a table at which they would eat. And the food was the same. Let me repeat that again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just now, sir, just so the record is clear, you -- you referred to or at least the translation came through in the transcript as you referring to 5 -- between 5 and 12, maybe sometimes 15 soldiers. And you were talking about prisoners; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 15.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, it wasn't so much the number I was asking about, sir, but it came across soldiers. And you were talking about prisoners at this time; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mention soldiers. I said there were 50, 60, or 70 soldiers and there were, as I said, there were prisoners and they went there freely. There were prisoners who worked. I said what sort of work they carried out. There were 5 or 12 of them, and it's possible that on occasion there were even 15 of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And these were the prisoners -- yesterday you used the phrase to describe them, you said -- you called them "free prisoners"; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could go to closed session -- private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said yesterday and again just now, sir, that the food -- you would go to the warehouse to get food. What warehouse are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I went to get food in the warehouse. I clearly said that food would be transported by lorry. Raw food would be bought to my restaurant, it would be prepared in my restaurant and then served. And to this very day I don't know where that warehouse was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, where did you understand, whether you knew the exact location or not -- what was your understanding of where this food was coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time it wasn't for me to think. I just had to do what had to be done, sir -- and it was important to have enough food, enough food to prepare, to cook. And where it came from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During this time, sir, were you feeding other people -- I know it was during war, of course. But were you feeding only Stela's soldiers and some of these prisoners, or did you still have -- and I'm not trying to be silly in saying this, sir. I'm really asking a question. Did you have other customers, other clientele who would come in off the street, as it were, and eat at your restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had cameramen from Croatian radio. I prepared food for them because my father has a farm in the vicinity of the town, and they would come because I always had stocks from my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, then apart from this radio or television crew, were you feeding -- normally feeding other persons apart from soldiers of Stela's unit and prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe some other officers turned up from the town defence who would sit down there, someone I didn't know, because I wasn't in the restaurant all the time because I had this other job which involved the civil defence to do. I usually did that in the morning. Maybe someone else turned up in addition to these men, but I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask in that regard just for a moment do you remember if any senior HVO officers or officials came to your restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I probably didn't see them, or maybe I just wasn't there at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Let me just mention a couple of names to see if it provokes any memories, sir. Did a man named Slobodan Praljak ever come to your restaurant during 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slobodan Praljak would come to the restaurant, but during the war -- during the first war with the Serbs. I saw him on several occasions. I could recognise him on -- by his beard. I could see him now too. He goes to the restaurant now. But I don't remember seeing him eating in the restaurant at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how about a man named Milivoj Petkovic did he frequent the restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw him, not in any of the wars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'll just ask you one more. How about a man named Bruno Stojic, the Minister of Defence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Bruno Stojic personally, but he wouldn't go there. Only after the war when he made -- built a building next to my house. But I never saw him in my restaurant in uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, the food that you were getting from this warehouse, did you have to pay for the food, sir, or was it just being provided to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't pay for anything. I received bread too, bread and raw food, potatoes, beans. I said a certain amount of sausage, fresh meat, chicken, and that's what we used to prepare food. I didn't pay for anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that a fair amount, a substantial amount of these food items were in fact coming by shipment from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't work at the customs, so I don't know where it came from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in fact some of the Muslim prisoners -- excuse me, some Muslim prisoners were actually used to unload the lorries, as you described them, or trucks, bringing food and other items to your Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were three or four soldiers who had been given these duties. They were from the base, and there wasn't a big warehouse in my building so, so not much could be brought. But it was very easy to unload these things. I didn't see prisoners unloading anything at any time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever know a man named Nenad Harmandzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nenad Harmandzic was a permanent guest of ours in the restaurant before the war. I knew him very well. And during the war -- during the war with the Serbs there was some wine. He would just drink wine. He would sometimes turn up. And during the break between those damned wars, I lost contact with him. I still see his brother and his sons today, but I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that sometime in approximately early to mid-July that in fact Mr. Harmandzic was one of the prisoners who unloaded trucks at your restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him. It may be someone told me that prisoners unloaded these things. My wife, if she had seen this, she would have probably told me that, but I never saw him unloading the lorries because I said I've lost contact with him. I haven't seen him since the end of the war with the Serbs, and he doesn't live far from my house, maybe 200 metres away. I said that his brother sometimes turns up, but I don't know what happened to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present, sir -- did you ever hear that on an occasion when Mr. Harmandzic was allegedly unloading a truck at your restaurant that he was badly beaten by a man named Ernest Takac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I wasn't there, and I didn't see that. But I probably would have found out what was happening in my building, in my restaurant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Sir, my final set of questions. I'd like to direct your attention to the first few days of July 1993. And this was a time when there was another large wave, if I can use that term, if you understand what I mean, sir -- another large wave of Muslims being arrested. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dates don't mean anything to me now. What happened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you recall what you saw happening in Mostar around that time? There must have been some days -- is it correct, sir, that there were some days when there was much more fighting and much more commotion, if you will, and activity in the city than on other times -- at other times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what activity you are referring, to military or ... ?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, military activity or, as I mentioned, large numbers of arrests being made.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, at that time my father and a friend of his were captured at the demarcation line in the Bulevar and he was taken to Gnjojnice to the prison there. He spent three days there. I think that was at the time that people were being expelled on -- by both sides, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any Muslims friends at that time who came to you asking to be protected or seeking help in some way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time, because those neighbours of mine, whom I mentioned yesterday, they were protected. No one touched them. And I didn't go anywhere else. And as a civilian, I was not in a position to protect anyone, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'd like the witness to please be shown Exhibit 509.2, which was a new exhibit which I handed out before court started today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, if I can ask you to look at the Croatian language version of that document. I'll give you a moment or two to read the document and then there's just a few questions I would like to ask you about it. Have you had a chance to read it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, having shown you that document, sir, let me go back to some of the questions I asked you a few moments ago. Does that assist you in recalling a time, between approximately the 30th of June and the first few days of July, when in fact there was -- there were a large number of Muslims being arrested during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Having read this document, I can see that the perpetrators in that group, who were wearing uniform but didn't have any insignia indicating which unit they belonged to. And at the end it says that it created a false picture, a false image of the members of the HVO. I think that this is just an illusion of theirs. If there were no insignia, then who knows who the perpetrators were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, you jumped a bit ahead of me, sir. My first question is: Does this assist you -- does this assist you in remembering that in fact a large number of Muslims were arrested during the first part of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were arrested. I said that both sides exaggerated. There was a lot of exaggeration from the left bank to the right and from the right bank to the left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you're talking -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I apologise. I didn't move around the streets, so I couldn't see these things. I said I had a job to do, and as a civilian I didn't get around the town very much.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the arrest, sir, there's also description in this document of approximately 22 Muslim civilians who had been killed during the same time. Did you hear anything about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were rumours. But I can't claim that I know that this happened now. But there were rumours. Rumours exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the locations that's referenced here is Pecina Street, number 101, if you recall or see that. Where is that location -- excuse me, where is that location and reference to your restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not Pecina, it's Ricina, not Pecina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if I mispronounced it, sir, my apologies. Where is that --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ricina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott. Can we go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I suppose, Mr. President, out of abundant caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Clark. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. ML, I have a few questions to ask you. When you were providing meals for the Vinko Skrobo unit, you were asked by Mr. Scott if your restaurant was open to anybody to just come in and seek a meal, and I thought your answers were not quite clear. Was the restaurant open generally with a menu available? Could somebody come in off the street and say, "I'd like a meal"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said openly and in public that no one could enter, especially not civilians, and there was nothing you could order. There was just one dish that we could make. And we knew roughly how many meals should be prepared, plus/minus five, how many prisoners, workers would come. And we cooked so many meals, plus/minus five, and no one could come from the outside, especially not civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, it would be more accurate really to describe your premises during the period of the conflict as a designated canteen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in one sense, because food was brought from the warehouse. You couldn't buy anything and you couldn't sell anything in those days either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: In relation to the area around where your restaurant was, were there any coffee-shops or restaurants operating for the general public?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: For ordinary people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a prohibition by the town's defence. There was a prohibition on assembly, so it was not allowed for such facilities to be open. There was a decree issued according to which all these businesses were closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. And if people came to your premises during the period of the conflict, could they sit there and drink coffee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they couldn't have a cup of coffee. And I said especially not civilians. There probably wasn't any coffee either, because there were periods when there was no electricity and no one drank it. That's for sure, in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And indeed there were probably periods where there was no coffee either, I can imagine. Can you tell me a little bit more about the food that you were talking about. Do you have any idea who provided it? I mean, it's quite a job locating fresh food when you talked about meat and chicken during the war. Do you have any idea where that food came from, who paid for it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a moment ago I didn't work for the customs, so I don't know where it came from. I can give you a document from the civil defence telling you where the humanitarian aid came from, but as for the food, I don't know. It came there in a truck in front of my restaurant. Where it came from, how it got there, I don't know. I wasn't interested in learning either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I accept that. But do you even know did a soldier drive the truck? Was it guarded by soldiers? Have you even a vague idea who actually provided the food? Not necessarily which country it came from, but which town it had started in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: A small car would come in front of my restaurant bringing the food needed for that unit. It wasn't a truck with a trailer that would unload from one restaurant to another. They just brought the amount that we needed for that occasion. Now, where the warehouse was, where the trucks were, where the food came from, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, tell me this, Mr. ML: You said that you were paid for cooking it and that it was your job or that of your wife to keep a record of how many meals had been cooked and that you had given those records to somebody. Now, I have two questions arising out of that. First of all, how were you paid for cooking and meals and by whom? And then secondly, who did you give the records to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is a misinterpretation. I wasn't paid for the cooking, nor did I say that. I said that I was a commander in the civil defence and I received a salary there. My wife was a member of the unit and she received a salary. She was a quartermaster. I explained yesterday what that entails. And she was a quartermaster and, therefore, her duty was to cook, just as it was the duty of other soldiers to go to the front. I did not receive any compensation for the cooking, because I didn't really do the cooking. I just assisted my wife.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I see. So your salary was as you described yesterday as a member of the civil defence and your wife as a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. quartermaster?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Very good. Yesterday you mentioned that you had a lot of cans -- canned or tinned food. And would that -- would you have -- would you make a distinction between the canned food and the food that you got from the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: The canned food was semi-prepared, like a goulash, a stew, if you understand what a goulash is. These were cans coming from all over the world, in all kinds of languages. You could read the inscriptions and you didn't know what was in them until you opened them. So we cooked them. What was no good, we threw away. What was okay, we used. Because all kinds of things were contained in them. This may be funny to some people, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was that food that you would describe as humanitarian aid?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't say "humanitarian aid" on it. I had the key from the local community, and I had the key to the room there where these supplies arrived. But on those supplies there was an indication that they came from humanitarian aid, and on these ones that we were talking about there was no such indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Very good. Now, there's obviously different sources of the cans. The food that came from humanitarian aid, was that marked "United Nations aid"? Was it easily identified as food that came from either the United Nations or the Red Cross or the various aid organisations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a red cross drawn on it, so probably one would easily recognise it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: How was that aid distributed? How did so much of it end up in your restaurant?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which aid do you mean? You mean the humanitarian aid? I don't know whether it was humanitarian aid. I told you that I received the food from the warehouse. Where it came from when it reached the warehouse, I don't know. I told you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think we're talk at cross-purposes, Mr. ML. Yesterday in response to questions about giving prisoners food, I think it was from counsel for the Defence of Mr. Martinovic, you said that you had a lot of cans at your place, a lot of them, and so you could give them away. And we've also heard that there were a lot of cans kept at the Vinko Skrobo unit. Where would these -- did these cans come from? I know you can't answer where the cans from the Vinko Skrobo unit came from, but where did the cans that you had come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that in the Vinko Skrobo unit there were cans stored, because they didn't know where to keep them. And there weren't that many cans. I didn't say there were a thousand. Maybe even 20 is too many. Because in those days who had a can, he could consider himself lucky. He had plenty to eat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think, Mr. ML, you've answered a lot of my questions now. Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge Diarra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have a very small question regarding the gentleman called Lopata and Himzo Gakovic. I didn't understand what you said in regard to that question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lopata. I said regarding him that his very nickname is an indication of what kind of a man he is. And I said that a month and a half prior to that he broke the windscreens, two windscreens of the car observed by Jakovic, who is a Muslim like he.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did he do to Himzo Gakovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: He broke his windshields with a rock in front of the court because he had a case, a trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is he a fool? Is he crazy? Or is he a criminal? That's what I'd like to know, because you used both terms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's better to say that he was a bad criminal and a very strong criminal. He could load a truck in half an hour. And he also liked to steal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's questions? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Two questions to follow up on Judge Clark's questions. Further cross-examination by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, there was a second part of Judge Clark's questions. You said there was a record of the shipments received and perhaps the food used. I take it you had to give some sort of an accounting.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Judge Clark asked you, who did you give those records to or what is your understanding of what happened to those records that were kept.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: The records are handed over to people bringing the food. You have to sign a kind of receipt for receiving the food and an order for fresh supplies. Now, who they gave these documents to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that in fact leads into my second question: You said on some occasion -- I think you said earlier that these -- the food would arrive by lorry. And then a few moments ago you said something about coming in a car. But in either situation, sir, approximately how often were the shipments delivered? Was it every day? Did they -- for instance, did a truck come every morning, or how often would these deliveries be made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: It -- the deliveries would come every 10 or 12 days. And according to our regulations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a truck is between 1 and a half tonnes to 20 tonnes, because you have to sit for a driver's licence. Whether you're driving a lorry of 1 and a half tonnes or 20 tonnes. So these are small lorry, actually, that didn't have refrigeration, and that is why they had to come often.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the final question, sir: Based on the frequency of the shipments that you just told us about, was there ever a time when there was a longer gap, if you will, a lapse of time, longer than the 10 or 12 day that is you said the shipments -- during which the shipments were regularly made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ML [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes the interval was 20 days. If there were fewer soldiers to feed. There would be less cooking and less consumption if they went away. If they went to the seaside or something, there would be less of them to feed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing to add, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, witness, for coming here to give your evidence. When the usher pulls down the blinds, he will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, any documents to tender at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The plan of the town, 236 -- D236.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I guess there's no objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So the document D236 has been admitted into the -- under seal. Are there any documents to tender on your side, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so the record is clear, the only document that the Prosecution used with this witness was 509.2. And we will not tender it at this time. It may come up with a future witness, but we're not tendering it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Before we have the next witness, Mr. Krsnik, you promised us that you would furnish us with the videolink list of the new witnesses by Monday. Now it is Tuesday. We are looking forward to receiving that list of the documents, because we have been seized with a motion filed by Mr. Martinovic's counsel for the videolink. I believe that all the decisions should be made concerning with the videolink issues, so that we could have a good recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. We have carried out our duty and written our motion. That was addressed to you today, so you will probably receive it later this evening or tomorrow. I have also had consultations and informed Madam Registrar of all the problems linked to the videolink, so that, Your Honour, we have filed a complete list of witnesses today. And as I see the witness coming in, I can give you a complete report of all the names proposed, in which there are very few changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, my question is: Have you indicated the length of the direct examination, what kind of protective measures you asked on this list?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, we haven't. But we can do that in a couple of minutes. These will be brief witnesses who will come to testify exclusively about facts in the indictment with reference to my client. And I hope that not one of them will take more than half an hour in the direct examination. These are highly specific witnesses. After all the evidence produced, we feel there's no need for any repetition and we have focussed only on particular facts emanating from the indictment, or rather, from the evidence produced by the Prosecution witnesses. What has been indicated in our motion is that a witness - we are not in closed session - but he comes under number 11. And as he was unable to testify live here in the courtroom, for reasons that you are well aware of - and this is also explained in the motion - we wanted to ask Your Honours for him to be allowed to come and testify live in the week of the videolink so that we assume that regardless of the cross-examination, that we will manage to finish with all those witnesses for three or four days on the outside and then we may have three or three and a half days left, and then we would still have one and a half days in that videolink week when we could call our witness who didn't have his passport or a visa and that is why he was unable to come. He was due to come prior to the last expert witness. All this is elaborated in our motion. And Your Honours, the duration of the direct examination is indicated in the first submission we made when we spoke about deposition witnesses. But that's no problem. We can do that this evening, to indicate the length of the testimony and which protective measures we would request. So there'll no be problems whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since you filed that motion already, I think we'd better act in accordance with that list at a later stage. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just to indicate for the record, we have not seen it yet either, so I can't respond to anything specific. But one thought occurred which I think might assist the Chamber and certainly will assist the Prosecution. It sounds as if, according to counsel, they contemplate very specific questions of these witnesses. He just said he believed that he didn't expect any of the examinations to last more than half an hour and to be extremely specific in nature. It would, therefore, be most helpful to, certainly the Prosecution, and I submit to the Chamber as well, if then in that case some very specific summaries could be provided, so that we can then prepare accordingly. The type of summary that we unfortunately saw all too much of, Mr. President, the witness was a -- lived in Mostar during the war and will testify concerning the Muslim-Croat conflict. That kind of summary is not very helpful. And so if it is in fact true that counsel knows now about the very specific questions that we would put to these witnesses, we see no reason why a very specific summary cannot be provide so that we can indeed do our part in trying to see if we can accomplish all these witnesses in a single week. We could potentially narrow our cross-examination and prepare on the specific parts of the testimony, if we were provided that information which by this, Mr. President, we request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we are not debating this issue. We have two witnesses, if I'm not mistaken, waiting outside. I'll just give you one minute. One minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wish to assist the Court and my learned friends opposite, so I only need a few seconds. You heard the Prosecutor elaborating on all the witnesses planned for video. He did so for you. He interpreted my witnesses for you benefit. So he is perfectly well aware of everything, as both of us here are in the service Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of justice, and that is our mission here, so I will certainly prepare a summary and provide him with it. That's all I need to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, thank you very much for you cooperation. Now could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we start, Mr. Par, would you please inform me whether this witness is granted with the voice distortion measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness hasn't requested voice distortion, only visual distortion and the use of a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Mr. Par. Examined by Mr. Par:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you turn to me, please, so that you can see me. Before we commence with this examination, I would like to inform you that this Trial Chamber has granted your request for protective measures, for your identity to be concealed, your name to be concealed, and for your face to be concealed. First of all, the usher will show you a list -- a piece of paper bearing your name. Could you have a look at the piece of paper. And if your name has been correctly noted down, could you just say "yes." We'll just wait for a minute for the usher to finish doing what he is doing and then we will commence. That's the piece of paper. Could you have a look at it now. And if your name is on it, just say "yes." Don't read it out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we go into private session for a moment, given that I will be asking the witness certain questions relating to his identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we could break here and come back five minutes earlier than usual, that is, five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Witness, we'll continue later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we'll start with the period of the Serbian aggression against Mostar. And could you briefly tell us what happened to you at the time. And I'm especially interested in whether you were, at the time, in the army, whether you were engaged militarily.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: At the time of the Serbian aggression, I volunteered to join the HVO. We were volunteers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please turn towards me, and I shall indicate whether you should slow down perhaps or speed up. Could you tell us which HVO unit you joined.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I was in the 4th Battalion. It was called Tihomir Misic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us who the commander of that unit was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Tihomir Misic was the commander of that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What duties did you perform in that unit? What sort of tasks did you have and what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I was an ordinary soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What duties did you perform? What tasks did you carry out within that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: My duties involved defending the town. We went to the demarcation line which separated us from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long you remained within that unit. Up until what date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I remained in that unit right up until the 9th of May. And in fact, even after I was captured -- only after I had been captured did I leave the unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the date of the 9th of May, 1993; is that correct? You did say "1993." And you said that some people were captured. Could you please tell us, what happened on the 9th of May, 1993 -- what happened to you? Where were you? What happened? Could you give us a brief outline of those events.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, on the 9th of May, that's the day on which I was captured. But right up until then there were regulated shifts, and the number of men who went to the demarcation line, which separated us from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just help you a bit. Tell us, on the 9th of May, tell us, where were you? At what location? Which other unit were you in at the time and how did this capturing take place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, I was on the line towards the Serbs. And in the morning hours we heard shooting. It wasn't clear to us. We didn't understand why there was shooting, why there was confusion, although a few days prior to that time there were certain incidents between Croats and Muslims at the Bulevar. There was already a sort of imaginary line, I don't know. But we could have assumed after two or three hours of shooting -- we could have assumed what was happening. But initially no one knew what was happening because the unit was mixed at the line. Half of the unit were Muslims and the other half Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you heard shooting. You assumed what was happening. But what did you assume? What assumptions did you make? What sort of conflict was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, these were just assumptions. We thought that perhaps a conflict had broken out, but no one believed that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Between whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Between the Croats and Muslim, because as I said, we were a mixed unit and until that time -- well, we didn't hate each other. We were together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you saying that in that unit of yours, half of the soldiers were Muslims and the other half Croats, have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened after you heard the shooting. You understood that a conflict had broken out? What did you do? And how did this capture take place, the capture that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The shooting lasted until about 12.00 or 1.00, when we called the command, which was located about 2 or 3 kilometres below us, we asked them for an answer. We asked them to tell us what was happening, because all we could do was guess. So we were told from the command to remain at our positions and not to withdraw. However, on our own initiative, because we could see that something was not quite in order -- on our own initiative we decided to withdraw from the line. And as we were descending from our position to the bottom -- to the foot of the settlement, to the village of -- to the settlement of Gnjojnice, we reached the houses, the population, and we asked the inhabitants to tell us what was happening, what sort of conflict was involved. They complained and said that they had no idea. They said that this conflict had broken out, and we said we just want to return home. We said, "What sort of a conflict is this?" And one woman told us that we shouldn't go -- we shouldn't go in the direction we intended to take. She showed us the route we recollected take to avoid BH army soldiers. We listened to her. And after we had -- we reached a small street after about 100 metres. We were stopped. There were men with rifles and Zoljas, and they told us to surrender ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were captured in Gnjojnice. Who captured you? Do you know which unit was involved? Do you know which army was involved? What did they tell you? Were you disarmed at that point? How did the events unfold after this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, we didn't know which army was involved. We could only identify the army on the basis of their insignia. They had BH Army insignia. And then we realised that they were Muslims because in the BH Army almost 99 per cent of the soldiers in that army were Muslims. And this wasn't the case in the HVO, where the composition was quite Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mixed. So we put our weapons down. They took our weapons from us. We asked them why, we asked them what was happening. And they said we would find out about all of this once they had taken us to the command in Gnjojnice. They took us there without our weapons. They took us there. And when we got to the command we asked why this had taken place because we weren't involved in any kind of conflict, and they told us that an attack was in course, that war had broken out. We didn't believe it at the time. They give us something to drink so that we could refresh ourselves, and then they asked -- established contact with Berto Pusic. However, that was not possible. And after a certain period of time they called their command. After that, certain people turned up. And right up until that time all our weapons, all our equipment remained in that command with those people I mentioned first. Afterwards these people took our rifles and put us into a -- into a refrigerated lorry and said they were taking us elsewhere. We didn't know where they were going to take us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll stop you there for a minute. Sir, there was one group of men in the command and they were looking for someone called Pusic. You said that they were looking for Pusic. Who was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, as I was a soldier, I personally don't know him, and I didn't know what the composition of those in power was. But they insisted on getting into contact with him and they said that they couldn't get into contact with him and they said that he was someone who could -- they said he was someone who could calm the situation down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then that second group took your weapons and they took you somewhere -- they took you away. Where did they take you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: There was another soldier, a BH Army soldier with us in the lorry. He was guarding us. And according to what he said, first of all they took us to the South Camp. But since the South Camp was being shelled, they couldn't leave us there and they said that as there was shooting, we should be taken to the city -- to the SDK, the public auditing service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does the SDK mean? Is that the name of a building? Where is it? Is it on the east or the west part of the town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The SDK was a financial transaction centre. It's in the eastern part of town, in the eastern part of the town of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how many of you were there in that group and were there both Croats and Muslims in that group.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: There were nine of us in that group. I can't remember exactly whether there were five Croats or four Croats and five Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So what happened when you arrived at the building that we have called the SDK building? What happened to you? Who did you find there? How were you treated? What did they -- what did they want?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: When we got to the SDK building, the tension there was palpable. They took our uniforms all. They said we didn't need them, they took our boots off. They took away our equipment. They searched us. But as Muslims -- but as Mostar is a small town and people know each other quite well, they started threatening the Muslims. They cursed our balija mothers. They said that we were traitors and they said, "Why aren't you with your people?" They even thought of killing them immediately. But later on it -- the situation calmed down a bit and it was said that they would move -- transfer to the BH Army -- they would be transferred to the BH Army and that was it. It was over then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the Muslims then accept to be transferred to the BH Army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I haven't finished. Then other people were brought in. This was on the ground floor. Then we were taken to the basement where that detention centre was. They then took our clothes off. They searched us. They searched for money, took things away. I had a little money on me. I had a cross around my neck. They started cursing my Croatian mother. They broke the cross. And then they shut us up in a room about 5 by 4 metres. And later on the Muslims who were with us didn't turn up, and four or five days later we heard them complaining. They said, "We're with you." And the most difficult thing for them was when they're exchanged. They had to remain there. They couldn't return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So you Croats were in that basement, in that detention place. You heard that there were Muslims who later on went into the BH Army. On that occasion were you beaten? Who beat you? Was everyone beaten? Did -- were you personally beaten by someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, when we entered the building and when we were searched, there were quite a few BH Army soldiers and almost all the prisoners didn't fare very well. Some fared better, some worse. But they didn't fare very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of them were there in that room? What were the conditions? What was the food like? Was it a real prison? What did it look like exactly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, when we entered that area, after we'd been searched, I saw that there were 20 people there. The room was 5 by 4 metres large. There were two small windows. It was a basement. It wasn't a classical prison. It was a basement where money was kept. There were two small windows. Men had been there -- they already arrived two days earlier on. We found that out later on in conversation. We found out who had been capture and there were civilians and not just soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's stop there for a moment. You said there were men who had been captured. They'd been there two days earlier. On 7th and 8th of May. Why were they captured? Who arrested them and why did you talk to them about this and what did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, yes, we talked about this, because no one understood why they were there, why they had been arrested since we'd been together until the other day. And then on the main high road and the Bulevar which later became the demarcation line there were people from the settlement, civilians and, some Croats who remained there, who were there two days earlier on. And they were there for security reasons. It would be best for them to be put away. And later we realised it was a Sunday when we were captured and it was Friday when we went to the line. Later it crossed our minds when we went to the line and asked the commands why the inhabitants who were there in a settlement in which the inhabitants were half Muslims and half Croats, we asked why they were making bunkers and fortification above their settlements while we were holding the line 2 kilometres away. We didn't understand why this was being done. They couldn't explain this. As I said, there was no explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the 9th of May, did you see these bunkers being used for military purposes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. Later they were operational. They were made operational.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us who was with you. Were they all Croats in that prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: In the SDK prison, yes, they were all Croats, every single one of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there women and children there, or only men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: In the SDK prison, only men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, was there another prison in the vicinity perhaps? Did you find out anything about this, a similar prison?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: When we were taken out to do work, we found out and we also saw that across the road about 100 metres -- 50 or 100 metres above us we found out that there were the fourth primary school there and we learned that there were civilians there, women and children too. They, too, were Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were personally able to see this when you went outside to work.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, we couldn't see this each time, but we wouldn't have learned this either, had it not been for a woman who knew someone and she told us that there was something there and said that if something happened or one of them got lost, she said she wanted people to know where she had been staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You just mentioned that you were taken outside to work. Can you tell us exactly what this involved. Did someone take you outside from the prison? Who took you outside? What sort of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, the patrols which consisted of three to five men took us out. They provided security. They said that we had to clear the roads, that we had to dig graves and do hard labour, physical labour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally go to do such work and on how many occasions and which locations did you go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, we went to do work almost on a daily basis. Certain individuals would even go two or three times every day. But the most difficult thing was the fact that there weren't many men a lot of men had been killed. The hardest thing was the dig the graves because we didn't have the necessary equipment, and you'd spend the whole day and the whole night digging.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, were you personally involved in digging graves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, on ten occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me please, where this was, at what locality, and do you know for whom these graves were dug?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The locality was the Osman Djikic monument and the theatre, and the graves were dug for the killed and for civilians and combatants, for all those killed. Only in some cases, if he was not a Muslim, we would bury the dead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me please, did you bury dead Muslims, dead Croats, or was there a distinction made as to who should bury who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Usually the Muslims buried their own because of the ceremony, and we would bury a Croat or a Serb or a gypsy if they happened to have been killed. We would dig graves for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, what were the conditions like? Was it life threatening? Was there shooting? How did they treat you, the people who had brought you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The conditions were wartime. There was shooting all the time. Shells were falling around us. We were not protected in any way. If it fell, it just fell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you abused, mistreated while working?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: There wasn't really serious abuse by the guards. There was more like provocations. The worst thing was when a large number of people would be rounded up and they had to run the gauntlet. They would be hit and insulted and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who would hit you, the civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, the civilians hit us. Actually, our escort would lead us into that crowd and then we would be powerless.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did those guards try and prevent the civilians from beating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. After five or ten minutes, they would intervene and say, "No one may touch you."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shall we go back to the prison at the SDK. Do you know whether there were any cases of the prisoners in SDK, their blood being taken?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. Four or five times they came looking for certain blood groups and requesting blood donors. They underlined that this should be on a voluntary basis. And then one or two men would go out, and after a few times they would come back and say, "We need more." So this was like a threat. So even those who didn't want to give their blood did. In fact, half the prisoners gave their blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For how long did you stay in that prison in the SDK in all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: 18 days. And in those 18 days, I lost 16 kilogrammes in weight.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fine. I don't mean if you lost weight, but thank you for your answer. Tell me, how were you released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: We didn't know about the release until the Red Cross came. And when the Red Cross came, they told us that we had nothing to fear, that they had made a record of us, that we had all been registered, and that each individual would be kept track of. And after that, we felt much more relaxed because no one provided any guarantees. After that the Red Cross would tell us that an exchange should take place soon. The Muslims kept saying from the beginning that they wanted an exchange but that your people don't want it. And then a couple of times they asked us whether we wished to join the BH Army, that we would do much better, that we would be much better off. But we didn't want to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when the exchange took place, how did it progress? Who took part in this exchange, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: We didn't know when exactly it would take place. We went to work, and around 8.00, after having worked for about an hour cleaning the streets, we were not aware what was going on but we were told that we had to hurry back to the prison. When we got there, there were people whose clothing had been torn or shoes torn. Then some supplies had arrived from UNPROFOR or the Red Cross and people whose clothing was in bad shape were given clothes to change into, and then they told us there would be an Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. exchange and we were happy to go home. And we waited for those lists to be compiled, the numbers to be checked to make sure that the Red Cross had everyone on the list, whether anyone was missing. Then we waited for about two hours, and then we were taken outside to the fresh air, and the atmosphere immediately changed. They behaved in a friendly manner saying that that is how it should have been from the first. And as we were waiting for the buses, more and more people were gathering there. We didn't know what was going on. The main street, the former Marsal Tito Street was full. There were between five, six, or ten thousand people. We didn't know what was going on. And then we learnt from the civilians that -- that it was an exchange all for all. Whoever wanted to return home, that they could, nor normal life to resume. And we continued waiting. People started getting nervous. And we were escorted by UNPROFOR APCs. The tension started increasing. People started beating on the buses, saying, "We won't let you go unless we go too." And then this APC was clearing the way, and there were a lot of buses planned for the civilians but only we were escorted across the customs bridge and transferred to the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me--?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: After this exchange I immediately went to hospital for examinations, and the next day or the day after I learned the civilians had not been exchanged at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, was all this in the presence of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. And the Red Cross were present too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You now arrived home. What happened to you? Did you stay on after that? Did you rest or did you have to become active again? What happened to you after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: When I arrived home, I met up with my family. I was very upset. I wanted to rest for a couple of days. However, tension was increasing. There was a shortage of manpower. The conflicts worsened, and I decided, though I didn't have to because the Red Cross provided guarantees that those who had been in prison could not be forced to join the army again -- but as from the beginning of the war, I was a volunteer member of the HVO and I felt sorry not to defend my people, so I decided to join again. And three or four days later I reported voluntarily to join a unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which unit did you join?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I joined the Mrmak unit. Half of my neighbourhood was in that unit. I knew the commander and I had heard that he was a good combatant, that he took care of his men. As I didn't have very good experience in the 4th Battalion that I had been in, and that was why I decided to join this particular unit and sign a contract with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the date when you joined this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date, but I can tell you roughly. It was in June, the 5th or 6th. I may be a week wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you knew the commander of this unit but didn't tell us what his name was. What was the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The commander was Vinko Martinovic, Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, so at the beginning of June 1993, when you volunteered to that unit, what kind of a unit was it? Had it already been formed? Did it have a name? How many men did it have? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The unit was composed of volunteers, people who lived in that town who loved the town and who wanted to defend it. That is why I joined that unit. As for Vinko Martinovic, Stela, I had heard stories that he had a good reputation from the war against the Serbs, that he had correctly treated his men, that he had been a good fighter, that his men had better equipment and weapons and food and accommodation, even during the war against the Serbs, that he took much greater care of his men than other commanders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, what was the name of that unit at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: We consisted of volunteers, so we had to give the unit a name, and so agreed that it should be called Mrmak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that unit later change its name and why and how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: After a certain period of time, a few days, a month - I can't say - the name was changed, because we had to be better organised, we could no longer be independent, we had to belong to the Ministry of Defence for the city, and we came to be called Vinko Skrobo. It was an anti-terrorist unit called Vinko Skrobo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the positions of that unit were and what its assignments were. Was it on the front, which part of the front?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The position of the unit, of the Vinko Skrobo unit, were along the Bulevar in town, and we just had to protect the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the usher will now give you a map. It is D2/38. And it is a map P14.5. Actually, it's a photograph of a certain area of the Bulevar. And when you look at it, you will show us where your positions were. Do you recognise this part of town and is that where the unit was positioned? Perhaps you can see better on the ELMO. And point to those positions with the pointer or the pen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The areas that we secured can be seen on this photograph, though the picture changes a little. This is newly built now. Part of the area that we defended was this area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please put a circle around that area with the marker.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in those days in 1993, when you were there, was the appearance of the city the same, or was it different? And what are the changes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The changes are vast. There's only a part of the old building that was left; this area here. Before, there was a dentist, a surgery here, and an emergency ward, and there was a much bigger building, three, four floors with the ear, nose, and throat ward. This is a new building, and also there was another part of the old building, a children's hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that is the area that this unit defended. Did this unit have a base somewhere else, and can you show us that spot on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The Vinko Skrobo unit did have a base, but it cannot be seen on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: It is about 400 to 500, 600 metres as the crows fly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you point in which direction, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Up here, further up. In this direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right next to you were there other units on the Bulevar? Which other units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. In addition to us, and next to us, to the left, was another independent anti-terrorist unit, Benko Penavic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other side, were there any other units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. The Domobrani Regiment, then Zolin Jajce [phoen], the military police and along the whole Bulevar like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, this Mrmak or Vinko Skrobo unit, did it ever move from these positions during your stay in the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No. From the first to the last day, it held the same positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the task of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The task of the unit was to secure the line and to prevent any crossings. So it was protecting the line exclusively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men did that line number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The number varied. At first there were some 40 of us. And later on, just before the truce was signed, the number increased. I don't know exactly. Maybe there was 60 or 70 of us on the outside, but this was only for a short period because after the truce was signed, and when the guards unit was formed, people switched to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, did Vinko Martinovic in those days have any rank, military rank?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not. We were all soldiers without rank belonging to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you address one another? As he was your commander, how did you address him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: We addressed him as we did before the war, using his nickname, the nickname he got in the war against the Serbs, chief, Stela, commander. Those who knew him from before personally would call him Stela.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the nickname that he got, what was the nickname?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Puki? What would that mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: As he was the chief, the number one. So like short form for Pukovnik or colonel. It was short for Pukovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you get the materiel that the unit needed from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I personally -- logistics was responsible for that, though I did go once -- no, twice, I think, to the Defence Ministry of the city and take the materiel that we needed. But mostly it was the logistics who was -- that was in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you paid in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. We received salaries. At first in cash, and later on we were given coupons which we could cash in banks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who paid out the salaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The Defence Ministry, which was situated in Grude for the entire HVO. That was their headquarters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone bring the money to you, to the unit, or did you personally have to go there to get it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: When we were given the cash or the coupons, his name was Zeljko Colak. He was the logistics man and he was designated to pay us our salaries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in this unit, did you have a barracks? Where did you sleep? Would you spend all day there? How did it work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: In our base, we didn't have any dormitories. It was not built as a barracks. We all came from the immediate vicinity, so it wasn't far for us to go home. We slept in our homes. And we didn't need any places to sleep in, and there were no conditions for that anyway. There was no barracks. Just a base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have shifts? How was your work organised, your duties? How were they organised? When did you have to come to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, normally one person cannot be militarily engaged around the clock, so we had to have shifts and divide the number of people into groups. But as we were short of men, the shifts lasted 12 hours. And then we would be 24 hours off, so we would all go to our own houses as we all came from the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, who decided what each one of you would do and which shift you would be in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: At first it was rather difficult. But as we ran -- as things became functioning more regularly, a person would be chosen to fix the number of men, which features had to be guarded in particular, if somebody should be upset, then someone else for some reason -- someone else would take his place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever the leader of a group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No. I didn't want that either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you spend most of your time in the base, on the front line, or on some other assignment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Most of my duty time I spent on the line, and the rest with my family at home. Only exceptionally when a report would come in that an attack was forthcoming, then we had to go as reinforcements. But we would be on the alert and not go to the front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you show us on this same photograph where you personally were, what you were doing and where you were standing when you were on duty.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I may perhaps be able to show you two positions. Because of these new buildings, it's quite different now. Here -- there was a bunker here, one bunker. Then inside upstairs there was another one. A third was in the pharmacy. A fourth here would be on the alert, waiting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, when you arrived, beginning of June 1993, were those positions already established or fortified, protected from enemy fire? Were these regulated defensive positions when you got there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: When I arrived, the positions were already regulated. The windows were covered with sand -- sacks of sand, so that we didn't have to work on further fortifications. The premises were quite secure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, where were those sandbags that you mentioned. Could you show us with your pen, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Here on the corner there was a bunker with sandbags; inside upstairs there were sandbags with holes for rifles; then here, too, there were sandbags; and also above this building, about 100 metres away there were sandbags forming a wall of a metre and a half or 2 metres. And we did this to protect ourselves as we came to the lines. We came in our own vehicles, so there were incidents with wounding taking place here, so we had to position a rope with carpets and blankets so that a sniper would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not be able to see us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How high was that rope with carpets, and what was their purpose?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The height was about 6 metres. I can't tell you exactly. And the purpose was to shield us as we came on duty, so that we couldn't be seen, because we had two people wounded there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
