utterances.text: Tell me, were there any anti-tank obstacles just below your positions? Were there hedgehogs or any kind of obstacles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, there were hedgehogs, here in front and there were some mines planted in front of the building too, so that the only way one could reach those positions was by road. And this was protected from sniper fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, can you please tell me, when you were at this line or on your shift, what was the usual practice? Did combat take place on a daily basis? How fierce was the fighting? Could you describe an average day at the line. What did you do? How fierce was the fighting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, there was no very fierce fighting at the line. There was sporadic shooting every day. But if you were at your position, if you were protected, there were no great threats, no serious problems. There was sporadic shooting on a daily basis, and maybe once or twice the Muslims attempted a break-through. But that's all that happened while we were holding the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, do you know who was on the other side? Naturally the BH Army was there, but do you know which units were there and who the men were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, we didn't know what the names of the units were. We knew that the BH Army was there. However, later we found out certain names, since the town is not a big town, so everyone knew someone else. So it wasn't hard to establish contact. And whose unit it was, no one talked about that. We didn't even insist on finding out -- finding this out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Apart from that task at the line, did this unit have any tasks in the town? And I mean did they have any tasks which involved checking up on Muslims, conscripts, checking their identity papers, arresting them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No. Our unit was only active in the Bulevar. Our duty was to protect that area, because that part of town was the one exposed to the greatest risk, and our task was just to protect that part of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And tell us please, in that part of town, near the medical centre, were there any crossings? Did Muslims cross over from the western part to the eastern part of town? Did you ever see anything like that happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Not on a large scale. The crossings that did take place were minor ones. And they had mostly been arranged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say what "arranged" means, what an "arranged crossing" means. Did you personally participate in anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, I did on one occasion. And a woman with two children asked me to help her. He said that Herman -- her husband was in Blagaj and that she was worried about what her fate might be, worried about her children. She said that he wasn't safe, she feared for her life, and she said that he would like to cross over. She pleaded with me for two days. I refused to help her. But two days later I told her that if you have a hundred per cent sure -- I asked her whether -- what her problems were, whether she was threatened by anyone. She said she was just worried for herself and for her children. I said, "If you are really certain that you want to cross over, I can arrange for your crossing and make sure that no one on our side will maltreat you. I will inform our men, and you'll be able to cross over." And this is what took place. I informed both the left -- my men on both the left side and on the right side, and then I called to the men over the road and told them not to shoot. I said that a woman with children would be crossing over, and this is where she crossed. She crossed over without any problems. And after a year, year and a half - I don't know how much time expired - but we met again and she thanked me. She said that she didn't have any problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is when the peace had already been signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, she had already returned to her flat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this a typical way of someone crossing over, this example you have mentioned? Was this a typical crossing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the crossings were of this kind. They had all been arranged as far as I know, if they took place on the line. I can only talk about the crossings that I observed when I was on shift, but I can't comment on rumours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in that unit of yours, were there any prisoners of war in that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were any prisoners of war taken to your unit? Were there any prisoners of war in the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: In which unit? Where?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the base.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. At the base, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were these prisoners? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The prisoners were people from the Heliodrom. On the whole they were Muslims, men who were fit for military service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how they got to the unit? Did anyone go to collect them and how many of them would usually arrive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: To -- well, to collect the prisoners, you needed authorisation from the Ministry of Defence in the town, authorisation saying that people were required, what kind of people, and then that would have to be authorised. And only once the documents had arrived, the authorisation had arrived, only then would -- I can't remember the name now, man who was in the unit, also involved in the logistics -- only then would he go to the Heliodrom and he would bring them over and take them back to the Heliodrom in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On average, how many prisoners would there be at the base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, these men weren't brought over on a daily basis. They were only brought over for certain types of jobs, when it was necessary. Then you'd go to -- and try and obtain an order. The maximum was about 20. Usually they'd ask for five or six men. And later on with their assistance they would insist to remain at the base for safety reasons and then they would be authorised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did some of the men remain there overnight?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Some men at their own request, they were concerned for their safety, as they said. They said it was better for them to work there and to live there than to be taken by some other group. And these were people from the town who knew each other, and they would then be left there and after a certain period of time returned and then they would be brought back again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do in the unit? Did you see what sort of jobs they did at the base?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, mostly they were involved in clearing up the area around the base, making coffee. They'd maintain vehicles, the cars that were used by the unit. As far as I know, they would fortify our cars. They were involved in emergency services. They'd repair the bodywork for security reasons. And then they would repair private cars. This was all done on a voluntary basis. And you'd buy them a drink for this -- you'd buy them drinks or buy them cigarettes. And -- well, just for the sake of it, we'd ask them whether they had to be paid, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they fed in the unit? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: They ate the same food that we did, but we didn't eat together. They got the same food from the same kitchen. We ate in the Hladovina restaurant, whereas they ate -- well, since there was an entire floor at the base which was there. They ate at the base, or once we had finished with our shift, et cetera, they would sometimes go to the restaurant too. But they wouldn't sit at the tables themselves, but in the garden.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, were they maltreated? Did I did anyone beat them, humiliate them? Did you see happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone being maltreated. Yes, perhaps there were verbal insults. This happened because of the pressure of the war. But I didn't see anyone beating them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, as far as you know, was anyone ever killed or wounded, any of these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: As far as I know, this didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have the occasion to see whether these prisoners were able to receive visits? Did anyone go to the base to visit them, family members, friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. There were visits, but we didn't really authorise that much because the base was also shelled sometimes. And for the sake of their security and our security, we didn't allow this. We would usually allow the prisoners to go home, or we would take them home, or we would allow them to go home on their own. And in the evening or the afternoon they would return themselves. That's the extent to which we trusted these people, and they would return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the prisoners sent to work at the medical centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No, they weren't. They weren't sent to work. Only in exceptional situations, if it was necessary for an electrician to come because the electricity supply had been cut off, an electrician would turn up to repair the fault. Or if it was necessary to clean the building that we used for accommodation and in which we slept, and that was in the upper part of the medical centre. So they were not at any risk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us on the map where this was and how it is that they weren't exposed to risk -- to any risk. Could you point to the location where they went.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, the third building can't be seen in this photograph, the third one that should be here. Behind it there was something like a club for alcoholics. And in that basement, we slept in the basement in the night shift. This is where we would rest and this is where we would make coffee and where we would stay if we weren't at the bunker, because later we went directly to the bunker. They would then clean it up and make coffee for us, and if there was a problem with the electricity, they would repair it, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us in what way you think they were protected. How were they protected from enemy fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, the building itself was well fortified. And in addition to that, they were in the third building, which was the furthest away. Well, you couldn't say that people were a hundred per cent safe there, but from the time we arrived there onwards, after the sandbags had been positioned and the screen, no one was wounded, nothing happened to anybody. And none of those prisoners who went there were ever exposed to fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one thing I'd like to clarify. In the transcript I see that you mentioned an alcoholics club. So in order to avoid misunderstandings, in order to clarify this, what was you referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: That is a place that we chose to sleep in in the evening. That's where we would sleep. Because we would go to the bunker in shifts, and once your shift was over we'd spend 12 hours there and then you would go away for two hours and have a four-hour rest and this is where we would sleep. This club where our dormitory was located, before the war those premises were used as an alcoholics club.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this used to be a club for alcoholics. That's why you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mentioned it. Sir, can you remember the 17th of September, 1993, when a large-scale conflict broke out at that demarcation line and a tank was involved in the conflict? Can you remember that event, and were you on the line on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that day because all the men from the unit, we were all soldiers and we were engaged. We were told that there should be some sort of coordinated action and that all the units at that line -- we were told that the line was to be moved. We received the order that we should all be in our positions, all the men from the units. We were only waiting for the tank to arrive. After an hour, the tank arrived. We moved the sandbags. We positioned them in the shape of a letter "V" so that a barrel could protrude from it. And after the tank had fired for a certain period of time, we were told that we should move on and attempt crossings. The tank fired two, three, maybe four shells -- two or three for sure. And then we received the order that when the shooting started, there would be an all-out attack, but we were told not to cross over. We were told that the tank was defective, that it couldn't follow us. We remained at our positions. And men to the right of us, they were from Livno, these men, they attempted a break-through. Immediately they tried to cross on foot. But whoever attempted to do this died. I think seven of them died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. And could you please point to the map and could you identify the position of the tank, where it came from and where it fired from.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, you can't see everything on the map, but it came from the Rondo, this part here -- this part above here. There were sandbags here. The tank came to this point. That's where it fired from.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you positioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I was in this building, in front.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of that action, did you move from that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No, we remained at those positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of the men from your unit move ahead?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Maybe three or four tried to go out, but later on it was impossible for them to return. That was perhaps five or six metres away. This part here was mined. We had to take the streets. But we were ordered not to go any further and remained at our positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where these men from Livno went. Could you show us where they were on the map.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: They were in the school, in the primary school. And they were supposed to cross into the Serno [phoen]. And they tried to do so --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did that last? How long did that action last?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The action -- well, 10 or 15 minutes, it felt, because we didn't progress. We stopped.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that day, in that action, were there any prisoners of war near the medical centre? Did you see that there were any of the prisoners of war with the troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Prisoners of war near the medical centre with the troops? No. Just the troops were there, members of the unit -- of the anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see whether any of the prisoners on that day were used in that area in front of the medical centre as a live shield?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No, because we were at the front line. We were to move ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see whether any of the prisoners was in front of your positions with wooden rifles? Did you see any prisoners in these positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No, no. There were no civilians, no prisoners there, just the troops.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see whether any prisoners were given uniforms and wooden rifles to make them resemble troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear at the time or later on people saying that this event took place, the event I have mentioned involving wooden rifles and prisoners who were used as a live shield?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: After a certain period of time, I heard a rumour that this had happened at the Bulevar. I heard that soldiers had been sent. There were millions of rumours, but they hadn't been verified. I personally didn't witness anything. And while the action lasted, I didn't see any civilians or any prisoners.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear any stories that is this happened in your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: After a certain period of time they said that our unit or other units were involved. All the units were in fact mentioned, whether you were in the 4th Battalion or the Benko Penavic unit or in our unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, could you please tell us, do you know someone called Nenad Harmandzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know someone called Halil Ajanic whose nickname is Lopata?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. I know lop that from -- Lopata from sight, from the town. But I'm not on particularly friendly terms with him. I never really struck up a conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in your unit, in the base as a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him at the base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sort of conditions you saw him in, how was he treated, how did Stela and the other soldiers treat him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Stela usually treated all the prisoners in a correct way. So I don't think there were any exceptions and I don't think Lopata was treated different. He was a bum, in fact, without a fixed come domicile, a drunk. He was a scapegoat in the town and people would laugh at him. That's how I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me whether you heard about the tragic event when somewhere in the vicinity of your unit, his son, who was a minor, was killed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that event. I wasn't there at the time because I was at the front line. But it was only a day later that I found out in a conversation what had happened. I found out that his son had been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you hear? What were you told? What was his relationship to --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, the nature of Stela's relationship to Lopata can be seen from the fact that children would turn up at the base and they would play there, they would hang around there. Someone could give them chocolate, fruit juice. So he was treated more like a civilian prisoner, not like a prisoner of war. So the children would always appear there and hang around. There was a German in the unit too, and the German took the little child with him all over the town all the time. They went out together all the time. And then allegedly, according to a story that I was told, across the road from the base, that's where the German lived and he had all his equipment in that flat, explosives, bombs. The little child went up to the floor. They were playing. I don't know what he were doing exactly. I can't say -- apparently a hand grenade was activated and he was blown up. And then the ambulance and the police and the on-site investigation was carried out. And then the German then was taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long you were in that unit as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I was a soldier in that unit right up until the truce was signed. And after it had been signed, maybe one month later, I asked about what would happen to me because we were to be disbanded. The war was going to be over. It was not such a fine source of remuneration. So I decided to leave the unit and to join the Guards Brigade. That was right up until February, I think, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: 1994. Witness, thank you. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it's almost time for the break. We have still two minutes left. So we'll break now and then we'll resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination. Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Bos:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness MM.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My name is Roeland Bos from the Office of the Prosecutor, and I'll ask you some questions as well. Witness, let's first talk about the members of the Vinko Skrobo unit. You testified that when you joined the unit, there were about 40 members and when you left or when the unit was dissolved there were about 60 to 70 members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: When I said there were 40 of us when I arrived, that includes me, so there were some 30 of us new members. That's what I meant. And before I left, the number increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So if I understand your answer correctly, you arrived with a group of 30 others. And at that time the unit had about 10 members. And when you with the group joined, there were about 40?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, the unit had been formed a couple of days prior to that. These volunteers that were securing the line and preventing the crossing of the BH Army to the other side. And I joined that unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, these first 10 -- maybe these first 40 members, were they all members -- people from the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say that later on the number increased, did it increase only with again soldiers from the neighbourhood, or did soldiers also -- other soldiers join this unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Mostly they joined upon recommendation. Because of the reputation of the unit and the authority it enjoyed, then one of the soldiers would recommend somebody to come and join, and that is how the numbers increased.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Vinko Skrobo unit ever had mercenaries in their unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've talked about the internal structure of the Vinko Skrobo unit, and you said that there were some group leaders. How many group leaders did the unit have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Specific leaders -- no one was nominated a leader, but they were chosen as shift leaders, people who would be responsible for the men, for the equipment. So somebody had to be chosen with authority. So within the shifts that we had - we had three shifts - there would be three men who would be group leaders. And then they would be replaced. When somebody had been enough, someone else would take his place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as you remember, could you give us the names of the men of which you know were group leaders.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I could mention five or six names. Dubravko Pehar, Ernest Takac. I can't remember the name -- nickname Dolma. He was also a soldier. Mladen Colak. Then Bozo Peric. I can't recollect all the names just now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And would it be Mr. Vinko Martinovic who would assign these group leaders, or were they chosen from the group? How did that -- who did the assignment of these leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The leaders were nominated amongst us. Nobody decided. We amongst ourselves decided that a certain person should lead the group and be responsible for this or that. And Vinko Martinovic left it to us, who would choose and whose orders we would respect while we were on the line.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I would assume that Vinko Martinovic, being the commander of this unit, would at least have to approve the assignment of a group leader; no? If he would not agree with the assignment, I suppose he would deny it; no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: It was left up to us, because the person who would lead us would be responsible for all of us, and we ourselves within the group chose the group leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned the Ernest Takac as one of the group leaders. Was he one of the members of the group of first ten members of the Vinko Skrobo when you arrived? Do you know when he arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I cannot claim with certainty, because he brought his group of men from his neighbourhood, because then there was us 20 or so. I don't know exactly myself, because I came then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that Ernest Takac took members from his neighbourhood. Where did he live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: He lived -- the district next to ours. And then his men in his group were from his district.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many men did he take with him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact number. I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the district. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you -- I don't know if you mentioned the name of the district where Ernest Takac came from, but could you repeat the name of the district, because we didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Ilici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And maybe while we have a map - and you've indicated already - on the Defence exhibit -- there's only the photograph here. But I think he also marked on a map. And maybe he can indicate on that map where this quarter is? Well, maybe we can come back to it later if the map cannot be found. Let me just ask you one other thing: Who was your group leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The leader of my group was Bozo Peric, Bozo. Dubravko Pehar as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was it first Bozo Peric and later on Dubravko Pehar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Dubravko Pehar was first. Then Bozo Peric. And then I don't know whether there was anyone else after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, what was the relationship between Ernest Takac and Stela? Did they have a good relationship, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Stela was fair and correct with all of us, so I don't know why he wouldn't be with him. But I cannot claim anything because I wasn't in his shift, that is, in Takac's shift. But as I was saying, Stela was correct to all the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me just understand the system. If you would work in a certain shift, you would always only see the soldiers of that shift. You wouldn't have any dealings with the other soldiers of any other shifts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No one would prohibit it. We all went to our own homes so that we didn't linger long, because we needed a rest, to see our family, then there was the line, the state of war. We didn't have much time to socialise, so we were programmed. Our working hours were fixed. We were very busy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it fair to say that members of the Vinko Skrobo didn't move around in the different shifts, they would always remain in the same shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: That is right. Only if upon a specific request, if somebody wanted to go to the other shift, he would be given permission to do that. But then someone else had to come from that shift so that the number of men had to be the same in each shift.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question about Ernest Takac. Do you know whether Ernest Takac was ever dismissed by Stela from the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've been given the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe we can put it on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if you can indicate the area where Ernest Takac lived. Maybe mark it with a number "3," I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Bos, I believe that this map is a new map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And we are in the open session, so it's not proper to mark it with number "3" if there's no number "1" and number "2."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour. I thought it was the Defence map. But if it's a new map --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe you could just indicate the area where Mr. Takac lived. I don't think we need to have --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If we're going to use the Defence map, we need to go into private session. I understand what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So maybe we can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, you'll be given the same map as before. So now I'll ask you to look at that map and indicate with a number "3" the area where Ernest Takac lived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this is a -- Exhibit P556 is a report from the military police, and it talks about the special status of the Vinko Skrobo and the Benko Penavic unit. And please read it -- read it by yourself, and then I'll ask you some questions about it. Have you read it? Witness, this document in the first paragraph talks about -- about two units, the Vinko Skrobo ATG and the Benko Penavic ATG -- or it says Branko Penavic. And it says these two units are listed as part of the Convicts Battalion. Now, my first question is: Is that correct, what's stated here? Were the two ATGs part of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No. We were an independent unit, ATG Vinko Skrobo, under the command of the defence of the town, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if -- to who would Mr. Vinko Martinovic report? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I personally never saw any documents or anything like that, but judging by everything, it was to the command of the city. They were responsible for everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the term "Convicts Battalion" in relation to the ATG Vinko Skrobo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No. I heard of the Convicts Battalion, but I -- not of any connections with it, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we move on in that same paragraph, it says that the two -- these two units, they had a special status for unknown reasons. And then it continues: "This special status is reflected in the fact that neither the military police nor any other law enforcement organ is taking any measures against the members of these units who commit crimes." Now, witness, is it correct that these -- the ATG Vinko Skrobo in Mostar had a special status in relation to the other units -- HVO units in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: We were an independent unit under the command of the city. That's how it was. Now, what privileged status is referred to here, I don't know. I'm not aware of any privileges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what does it mean that you are an independent unit? What does that make you different from the other units in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: All the units were more or less independent. They consisted of smaller parts, and then they gave themselves these names. They organised themselves independently. But they were all under the command of the city. They all belonged to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, it says here that -- that the ATG Vinko Skrobo and the ATG Benko Penavic, that the military police had less control over these units. Was that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I can't claim that because the duty of every military police is to control the troops. Now, why wouldn't it do its duty?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you've testified that one of the reasons why you joined the Vinko Skrobo unit was the fact that -- that they had better equipment and better food and better organised. Did that have anything to do with the special status that this unit had compared to the other units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: A special status? An independent unit organised everything. It depended on the men, how capable they were to collect donations, who would be the donator, who would get the equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say who would be the donator. And who was the donator for the ATG Vinko Skrobo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: There wasn't one particular donator anywhere. There were several donators, well-off people who had their own businesses, shops. They gave their contributions. They were not militarily engaged and they were able to continue with their own business, so they assisted the units as best they could.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you give us some names of people or organising who donated to the Vinko Skrobo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: These were all private entrepreneurs. There wasn't a fixed sum that someone had to give. All of this was on a voluntary basis depending on how much people could afford either in money or food or drinks. Nobody prescribed how much people should give. These were voluntary donations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: And they all came from the areas in which we lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you're avoiding to give an answer to my question. I'm asking could you give us some names of people who actually donated to the Vinko Skrobo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, because I didn't receive those donations. I didn't have control over them. But there were stories, rumours, shops, commercial establishments that were helping us. So virtually everyone took part. There were no exceptions. There are letters of gratitude that can still be seen in shops to this day for this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if these donations were given, who would they give the money to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I haven't got a clue. I wasn't a member of the logistics team and I wasn't aware of these matters. I was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, I've asked you twice to give us some names, and you still didn't give me any names. And in your last answer you said that virtually everyone in the area took part. Now, again, if virtually everyone took part, could you give me at least some names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you want, we can go into private session, if you think it will reveal your identity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, when I asked you where that money would go, you said it went to the logistics team. Who was a member of the logistics team in the Vinko Skrobo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I can't say for sure whether logistics received that or not. All I can say is that I can assume this. I was a soldier. I wasn't informed about these matters, and it wasn't my job to be involved in such matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, earlier in your testimony - I'll have to go back - I think you spoke about logistics as well and then you mentioned a name Zeljko Colak. Could he be one of the persons involved in this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I have no idea. It wasn't my job. And I wasn't interested in that idea. And Zeljko Colak, yes, he was in the logistics team in the unit of which I was a member too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, while we're on the topic -- just again you testified that you got paid. How exactly did you get paid? Could you explain that to the Court again, how would that -- how would that work.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Every soldier in the unit was paid. At the beginning we received cash. And after a certain period of time, we were given coupons, vouchers Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. for our salaries and we would collect money from the bank. And the money came from Grude, from that operative centre there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that this Zeljko Colak was the one who was actually giving you the slips and giving you the money?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's return to the exhibit. In almost the last paragraph, it says the following: "I would like to point out that of the entire personnel of the above mentioned units, a large part is involved in criminal activities." Witness, did you know that members of the ATG Vinko Skrobo were involved in criminal activities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No, I didn't. And I don't know any member who was involved in criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P707, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the next exhibit which I'm going to show you is a very big SIS report, a report from the security and information service, and it's addressed to the chief of the SIS, Mr. Miroslav Tudjman, and it's dated 4 December, 1993. In this report, the report is on the findings of crimes that were committed in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And one of the chapters in this report lists crimes that were committed by the Convicts Battalion. And that's the chapter which I would like you to refer -- which I would -- want to refer to. And if you could please move -- in your original version, you see on the right-hand top you see a number, and I'd like you to move to number 01029711. It's probably all the way in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And the usher left the courtroom, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see the number in the right-hand corner? So you should go to the number where the last four digits are 9711.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: For the English version, it's page number 43.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it seem that the English version has lost the numbers on the bottom. So the English version ends with 0446. Witness, do you have that in front of you? The heading says the "Convicts Battalion"? Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes. Something is not clear to me. What does this have to do with the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that. We'll get to that, witness. And I'll read it out, that first sentence. It says: "As you requested, we are sending you a report on our findings on the illegal activities of members of the Convicts Battalion. But we would like to point out that these are only cases from sources we have found to be reliable." Now, if you then turn to the sixth paragraph on your page, which starts with "At about 10 hours on 21 September." Do you have that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just read that paragraph, and then I'll ask you some questions. Witness, this describes an incident where a woman is being beaten, and it says that there were members of the Vinko Skrobo unit involved. And it mentions two specific names, Mr. Semir Bosnjic and Mr. Nino Pehar. Do you know both of these persons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Nino Pehar, that the person who was your group leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: He -- there was one such person, but not in the shift that I was in. We didn't have any contact. We were members of the same unit though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But Nino Pehar is not the same as Dubravko Pehar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Semir Bosnjic? Was he in your shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall that this incident took place, which is described here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen this, the first time I've heard about this incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you want to now move to the next page and read the third paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In the English version, it's on the bottom of the same page, which starts "On the 29th September, 1993, in the evening."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, this is just a short paragraph. And it talks about the fact that Muslim civilians were expelled from a neighbourhood called the Centar II. And this was done on the 29th of September, 1993. Do you recall that this took place and that the ATG Vinko Skrobo was involved in this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: This is the first time I've seen and heard about this too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So -- all right. Very well. And then if you could move on on the same page, the sixth paragraph, which is a bit longer, that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And on the English, it's the bottom -- it's the bottom paragraph on page 20449. And this paragraph starts with "Following the order of a department."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall that this incident took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No. This is the first time I've had the opportunity to read this too, and none of it is clear to me. This is first time I've heard about this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the man named Miro Bosnjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is he a member of the Vinko Skrobo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We'll leave the document aside now. Witness, you've testified that you knew a man named Lopata and that you saw him at the base -- the Vinko Skrobo. Do you recall when that was that you saw Lopata at the Stela's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I saw him two or three times before going to the shift or after returning from the shift. But as for the date, the time, a lot of time has passed since then, so I don't remember them. On each occasion I saw him in a normal condition, and I mean to say he hadn't been maltreated, he hadn't been injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there a lot of time spent between the very -- the three times that you saw him, or was it all in a short period of time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, that was a long time ago, so I can't make claims which would be a hundred per cent certain. Maybe it was ten or two days or three days. I really can't find my bearings, given that six years have passed since then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember a man by the name of Mustafa Sukaric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I don't know that name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, you've testified that you said that the Vinko Skrobo unit did -- never used any prisoners at the confrontation line. Did any of the other units that were holding the line adjacent to your unit - so I think on the left side or -- yes, on the left side it would have been the Benko Penavic, and on the other side the military police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The Domobrani and the military police. That's what the other line looked like at the Bulevar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any of these units use prisoners at the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: There was nothing else we could do at the line. We could only observe. And we couldn't abandon our positions and walk around. That was our duty. And as for going to other units to question people and to try and find out what everyone was doing, we didn't do that. We had to hold the line, do our shift, and after the shift go home. If you were on the alert, then you'd go to the base and wait there. Otherwise you'd just return home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that you never saw any prisoners on the Bulevar, either left or right or in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: What do you mean that we never saw any prisoners?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, saw prisoners working at the confrontation line. That's what I mean, to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: At the confrontation line. But where at the confrontation line?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in your -- in the immediate vicinity of where the Vinko Skrobo was stationed. I presume that if you were there, you could also have a look at the Bulevar and see what was happening on your left and on your right. Am I -- am I not correct in that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No. Because it was impossible to see. Each man had his area, and each man was responsible for his area. As for seeing what others were doing, it was impossible to see because we were all fortified. We couldn't even see each other. We had field telephones which we used to communicate, and if there was anything to communicate, we did it via the wire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Bos, could you ask this witness if he ever saw a prisoner at or near the confrontation line at any stage when he was holding his position. Make that absolutely clear. If you put the question to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, did you ever see a prisoner at the Bulevar from where you were -- from the position where you were stationed, did you ever see any prisoners on the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes, but behind my back, in exceptional situations. When we needed the electricity to be connected or we needed the premises to be cleaned. But at the positions that we occupied, no, they never approached these positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at the confrontation line, did you -- was your main task a defensive task or also an offensive task?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bos -- I'm sorry, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think there is a certain amount of confusion with regard to the confrontation line. Perhaps we could clarify this. If questions are being asked about this confrontation line, what is this considered to be? Because I see that the witness is a little bit lost, because this line could involve other parts of the town in depth. So since this could be a matter of confusion, I suggest that when questions are asked about the line of confrontation, I suggest that we define what this means exactly and what the area involved is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Par, the question that I put was whether he ever saw any prisoners at the confrontation line from the position which he held, and I think the evidence has been that his position was at the part of the Bulevar which the Vinko Skrobo unit occupied and no other part. So that's all we're interested in. Did he ever see, and he said he didn't. He saw the prisoners but they were way back in the building which he pointed out to us. So that's his answer. I don't think there's any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, when we left off, I asked you whether your unit was only involved in defensive operations or also sometimes in offensive operations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The purpose of our unit was for defensive actions. Throughout the war we were at the same position. We didn't move from our positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, for example, you gave evidence about -- about the actions on the 17th of September. And would you not agree with me that this was an offensive action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. It would appear to be an offensive action, because the entire line, all the units, the action was coordinated -- the action for the defence of the town, not our action. Our responsibility was the medical centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did these coordinated offensive actions occur more often, or was the 17th September the only coordinated offensive action in which you were involved?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: That was the only one, the only action which was coordinated, the only action in which an attempt was made to achieve something. Nothing else. There was nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, you -- I think you've given this evidence, but I'd like you to do it again. Could you give us exactly the names of the units which were involved in this coordinated action.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: A precise list of all the units -- of the names of all the units? I'm not authorised to do so and I don't even know about it. But according to what the commander said, the whole line from the Hum Hill to the Franciscan Church right up to the old secondary school and perhaps further on. Each unit participated in it, so the entire line which was held in the town. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who organised this joint action? Who initiated this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No, I haven't got a clue. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I assume that if you have a coordinated action or a joint action, there would need to be one person who would have some sort of overall command. Did you know on that day who had the overall command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I was a soldier. I only know who my commander was. But who the overall commander for the line was, I had no access to such information. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the time -- at what time the operation started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: At what time you mean? I know that perhaps it was 10.00, 11.00, 12.00. A lot of time has passed since then. I can't remember any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was your commander on that day? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Well, our unit was under the command of Vinko Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can -- you can confirm here that Vinko Martinovic was -- on that day was at the health centre.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The leaders of the groups had Motorolas, so that we used -- we heard his voice on the Motorola. And where exactly he was, I don't know, because I was at that position, as I showed you on the ELMO -- I was in the front part of the building, so the only solution for me was to observe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me put it differently, then. Did you see Vinko Martinovic on that day at the health centre at any time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I can't remember now whether I saw him then. I would see him every day. If that had been four or five years ago, maybe I -- maybe I would have remembered it if it was four or five years ago. But if you ask someone six or seven years -- about something that happened six or seven years ago, well, I really can't make any claims of which I'd be certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But if you say that you would see him every day, would you see him every day at the health centre? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No. He was positioned in his base that was under his command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, you talked about a tank. And I'm going to show you a photograph which the Chamber has not seen yet either. We recently discovered this. It's a somewhat older photograph of the area in front of the health centre. And it's -- it's a photograph of -- taken in January 1996. And it may be a bit more helpful for the witness to see this photograph. I'm afraid I only have one copy, but maybe we can put it on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And we'll provide the Defence with copies of this photograph later on, if that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Does that photograph have a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, it's marked P14.20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, how do we know that it was taken in 1996? Could that be explained to us. I haven't seen the photograph, but on what grounds does the Prosecution claim that it was in 1996 and why in 1996 in particular?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let the witness have a look at this photograph. Maybe -- maybe that will solve the problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, if you look at this photograph - and you can compare it with the photograph which you have seen before and which you have right in front of you - is it correct that this maybe reflects a little bit better what the situation was at the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you indicate approximately -- indicate where the differences lie.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The difference -- the neighbourhood -- I don't know what difference you mean. There are parts that have been newly built, a newly-built part of the health centre, and this is just a part of it, and some of it was set on fire. I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the part of the health centre that we see on this photograph, is that the old part or is this already the new part of the health centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: This is the old part where the emergency ward was and the dentistry department, before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you look at the photograph, right in the front of the health centre there seems to be -- I don't know how you would say it -- some sort of shed, some poles with a roof on it. Was that something which was there at the time of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "the covered area." I don't know what is implied.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, nothing is implied. I'm trying to find out -- if you have the building of the health centre, in front of it you see, is a construction, which you see on poles. At least that's how it looks like. Do you see what I mean? Maybe you could describe it as a covered walkway in front of the building.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. But this photograph is not a good one. I lived in this town. I was there throughout the war. I have no idea what this roof is. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: It was all shut up in front. There were sandbags. I don't remember seeing this even before the war, never mind after the war -- during the war. I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Par.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So as to avoid any confusion regarding this roof, I think this is a branch of the tree forming a kind of semicircle that looks like a roof. So I'd like to avoid any confusion, because there's a branch of the tree making a semicircle that one might think was some kind of an awning or a roof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that it looks like a fountain in the -- in the middle of the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we'll leave it. Maybe could I just ask one more question about this photograph. You talked about a tank on -- that was -- that assisted you on the 17th of September. Where was the tank located? If you need to indicate it on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think it would be easier, Mr. Bos, if you were to say where did the tank come from and follow the route of the tank, if he can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So witness, you've heard the Judge's question. Could you indicate on the photograph where the tank came from and where did it go to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: The tank by its sound and by the shots that were fired, it didn't appear in this area on the photograph at all. It was behind our backs. But I can't show you that position on this photograph. I could show you on this big photograph where the shooting came from, but not the direction in which it moved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that the tank never got anywhere in this area during this operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Would you explain to me -- in the operation the tank appeared. But this photograph that I have in front of me is not an area in which it appeared in at all, so it didn't appear in this part of the town at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that was my question, so you've answered my question. Witness, on the 17th of September, the units that were left and right of the Vinko Skrobo, I think you've testified that on your left side there were soldiers from Livno and you testified that these soldiers were crossing the Bulevar during this operation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes. They crossed. The operation was to have been coordinated. After two or three shells were fired, we were meant to see where the return fire was coming from and silence it if there was further response. But the communication amongst us was poor, so that the men from Livno, though our orders were not to move, to stay in our positions, they tried to cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from where you were, did you actually see the soldiers cross the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that during this crossing several soldiers got wounded and killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear whether also prisoners or detainees got killed during this crossing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No. As far as we knew, there were only soldiers with us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, was the operation a success?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM
utterances.text: No. The operation was quickly halted. It was -- it failed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will move to another topic, but maybe this is a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I have to remind you that you have to stay here overnight. So during your stay in The Hague, do not talk to anybody about your testimony and do not let anybody talk to you, because you are still under oath. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And tomorrow we'll sit in Courtroom I at 12.00. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I don't want to bother you. I just wondered if I could be given this photograph to review it, just to look at it, and then I'll tell my learned friend whether I need a copy or not. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: After this sitting, you are entitled to have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And we can provide copies to the Defence by tomorrow. I think we have spare copies in our offices. It's just that we only had one here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, but let Mr. Krsnik have a look first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Otherwise he could not go to sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
